summary: Re-read the sources for the 13 entries sweep 12 adjudicated and never merged, then refute the ones that pass
logs: 2 quotes no longer match the page · 4 verdicts changed from the brief
6 entries claim a pass — attacking each

recovered.name: K8s CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Forbid/Replace
recovered.verdictChangeReason: Verdict unchanged, but scope sharpened: the brief's quote and PASS_ABSOLUTE rating are fully earned by Forbid (no Job object → no Pod → no request ever forms). Replace is bundled under the same entry title but rests on a weaker guarantee — Kubernetes only promises the killed Pod stops running, not that any model request it had already dispatched gets un-billed. Kept as one PASS_ABSOLUTE entry since the quoted claim is about the skip case, but the reasoning below flags Replace as the softer half.
recovered.reasoning: Mechanism at the token level: on each schedule tick the CronJob controller asks only "does an active (non-completed) Job object from this CronJob already exist?" If yes under Forbid, it does not create a new Job — no Pod, no process, no HTTP call, nothing sent to any model. That's a structural zero-request guarantee, not a discount on an identical request. Quote (kubernetes.io, "Concurrency policy," confirmed verbatim on 2026-08-17): "Forbid: The CronJob does not allow concurrent runs; if it is time for a new Job run and the previous Job run hasn't finished yet, the CronJob skips the new Job run." The check is Job-status/time-only, never content-aware, so it cannot distinguish "redundant duplicate" from "distinct work that happens to overlap." It stops holding the moment the job isn't idempotent — the docs say so themselves, in stronger language than the brief's note: "A CronJob creates a Job object approximately once per execution time of its schedule... there are certain circumstances where two Jobs might be created, or no Job might be created... Therefore, the Jobs that you define should be idempotent." So even the skip is approximate, not guaranteed. Replace is the weaker half of this entry: it kills an already-running Job/Pod instead of preventing one from starting. Kubernetes' guarantee ends at "the Pod stops running" — nothing in the controller retroactively cancels a model API call that Pod had already dispatched before being killed, so a kill-after-dispatch pays for the discarded run's tokens on top of the replacement's, which is a cost increase, not a saving, in that window. The claim survives only for the invocation that actually reaches the model (Forbid's skip, or Replace when the kill lands before any request is sent) — never as a blanket "duplicate spend can't happen" guarantee.
recovered.savings: UNQUANTIFIED — bounded above by the cost of one full duplicate invocation avoided per overlap event; depends on job runtime relative to schedule interval (how often ticks would actually overlap) and per-call token cost. Can go negative for Replace if the killed run had already dispatched a billable request.
recovered.provenance: primary-doc (kubernetes.io official CronJob concept page, versioned for v1.36)
recovered.telemetrySignal: Observable without reading any request/response payload: compare the CronJob's `.spec.schedule` ticks against its Job object history (`kubectl get jobs` / K8s API audit log / CronJob events). A Forbid skip shows as a schedule tick with no corresponding Job creationTimestamp; a Replace shows as a Job deletion event immediately followed by a new Job creation at the same tick. Purely object-metadata and timing — content-blind.
recovered.quoteNow: Forbid: The CronJob does not allow concurrent runs; if it is time for a new Job run and the previous Job run hasn't finished yet, the CronJob skips the new Job run. Also note that when the previous Job run finishes, .spec.startingDeadlineSeconds is still taken into account and may result in a new Job run.
recovered.trap: Time-overlap-only detection with no content check, on top of Kubernetes' own disclaimer that scheduling is "approximately once" and Jobs "should be idempotent" — the mechanism can silently drop necessary distinct work (Forbid) or double-pay for a killed in-flight call plus its replacement (Replace). Passes only when the job is independently known idempotent and, for Replace, when kills reliably land before any model request is dispatched.
recovered.settlingExperiment: Point a CronJob's Job at a script that makes a real (cheap) LLM API call, set concurrencyPolicy: Replace, and engineer a tick where the previous run is mid-request when the controller replaces it. Check the provider's usage/billing log: if the killed run's tokens were billed despite its output being discarded, Replace nets a wasted call rather than a saving for that overlap.

recovered.name: BullMQ job deduplication (Simple Mode)
recovered.verdictChangeReason: Verdict upheld, but on stronger footing than the brief had. The brief cited only docs prose; I traced the mechanism into BullMQ's own Lua source (addStandardJob-9.lua + includes/deduplicateJobWithoutReplace.lua) on GitHub master. The dedup check runs and returns BEFORE storeJob()/addJobInTargetList() — a colliding-ID job is never written to Redis, never enters the wait list, never reaches a worker. That's a structural "no request was ever sent" fact, not a vendor assertion, so it isn't capped at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY the way an LLM provider's own claim about their internals would be: BullMQ is OSS running client-side under the customer's control, fully inspectable. Also corrected: star count is now 9,303 (brief said 9,279 five days ago — normal growth, not a red flag), repo pushed_at 2026-08-17T14:34:27Z (pushed today, clearly active), MIT confirmed. Page's own Last-updated timestamp is 2026-07-31, so the doc text predates and is unchanged by the 2026-08-12 sweep.
recovered.reasoning:
Mechanism, at the level the model reads: addStandardJob-9.lua calls deduplicateJob → deduplicateJobWithoutReplace before storeJob() runs. In Simple Mode (deduplication.id set, no ttl) that function does an atomic `SET dedupKey jobId NX` in the same Lua script; if the key already exists it XADDs a `deduplicated` event and returns the ORIGINAL job's id immediately (line 102-104 of addStandardJob-9.lua: `if deduplicationJobId then return deduplicationJobId end`). storeJob() and addJobInTargetList() — the calls that make a job visible to a worker — never execute for the second call. No job record, no dequeue, no worker pickup, no call to the model. That is exactly the "no request was ever sent" structural case the register's own rubric names as sufficient for PASS_ABSOLUTE, and here it's verified in source rather than taken on faith.

The quote: docs.bullmq.io, Simple Mode section, verbatim as of read: "as long as the job remains in an incomplete state (neither succeeded nor failed), any subsequent job with the same deduplication ID will be ignored." Matches the brief's quote exactly; not a paraphrase.

Where it stops holding: Simple Mode has no replace/merge path. A colliding dedup ID doesn't queue-and-catch-up the second job's data — it discards it outright. The library never checks payload equality, only ID equality, so the entire savings claim rests on the caller assigning IDs that are actually 1:1 with true request-identity. Get that wrong and the "savings" isn't a skipped duplicate call, it's a silently dropped distinct request — a correctness bug wearing a savings entry's clothes. Separately, this buys nothing on the (usually larger) set of non-duplicate jobs: those run with the exact same prompt, same model, same thinking as if dedup were off. The size of the prize is entirely a function of how often the caller's own workload actually submits true duplicates while the first is still in flight — BullMQ neither measures nor bounds that rate.
recovered.savings: UNQUANTIFIED — scales linearly with the caller's own duplicate-submission rate (× per-call cost of the skipped model invocation); BullMQ exposes a `deduplicated` event to count it but does not report or estimate a rate itself. Non-duplicate jobs see zero savings.
recovered.provenance: primary-doc (docs.bullmq.io, vendor's own docs) corroborated by a structural/source-code argument (BullMQ's Lua scripts, taskforcesh/bullmq master, read directly from GitHub) — stronger than the brief's doc-only citation.
recovered.telemetrySignal: Not observable as a distinct signal from a content-blind audit of the LLM provider's own request log. A deduplicated submission generates zero bytes on the wire to the model — indistinguishable, from the provider side, from "the application simply didn't need to call the model that time." Attribution requires the customer's own BullMQ instrumentation: counting `deduplicated` events emitted by the queue (jobId retained / deduplicationId / deduplicatedJobId) against total `queue.add()` attempts. Without that app-level event log, all a blind audit sees is a call-volume number lower than job-submission attempts, with no way to say why.
recovered.verifiedAgainst: 2026-08-17 (fetch date); page's own stated Last-updated timestamp is 2026-07-31T06:50:34Z (docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/deduplication, predates and is unchanged since the 2026-08-12 sweep); GitHub taskforcesh/bullmq: pushed_at 2026-08-17T14:34:27Z, stargazers_count 9303, license MIT (via GitHub REST API, read 2026-08-17)
recovered.quoteNow: docs.bullmq.io, Simple Mode section: "as long as the job remains in an incomplete state (neither succeeded nor failed), any subsequent job with the same deduplication ID will be ignored." (A near-identical but distinct sentence exists in the separate Throttle Mode section — "any subsequent job with the same deduplication ID customValue added within 5 seconds will be ignored" — do not conflate the two; the brief's quote is the Simple Mode one and matches verbatim.)
recovered.trap: Simple Mode has no replace/merge: a dedup ID reused across payloads that aren't actually identical doesn't queue the second job for later, it discards its data permanently. A savings technique becomes a silent data-loss bug the instant the application's ID scheme drifts from true content-identity — and the library gives no warning when that happens.
recovered.settlingExperiment: Instrument the queue's `deduplicated` event alongside every `queue.add()` call in a production window; divide deduplicated-event count by total add() attempts to get the real duplicate-submission rate, then multiply by the per-call cost of the model invocation that would otherwise have run. That is the only way to turn the UNQUANTIFIED savings into a number — it cannot be derived from BullMQ's docs or source alone, only from the caller's own traffic pattern.

recovered.name: AWS SQS FIFO MessageDeduplicationId
recovered.reasoning:
Mechanism at the token level: MessageDeduplicationId is checked only at SendMessage time. If a producer's SendMessage call times out ambiguously and the client retries with the same dedup ID (explicit, or the SHA-256 of the message body under content-based dedup) inside the 5-minute window, SQS silently drops the second SendMessage instead of enqueueing a second message. Exactly one message ever reaches the worker, so exactly one, byte-identical LLM request goes out — the surviving call is unmodified. Quote (verbatim, confirmed 2026-08-17): "If you retry the SendMessage action within the 5-minute deduplication interval, Amazon SQS doesn't introduce any duplicates into the queue." — from the "Exactly-once processing in Amazon SQS" section of the FIFO queues page.

Where it stops holding: this only guards the enqueue side. AWS's own visibility-timeout page states FIFO queues still run on the at-least-once delivery model: "In both standard and FIFO... queues, the visibility timeout helps prevent multiple consumers from processing the same message simultaneously. However, due to the at-least-once delivery model of Amazon SQS, there's no absolute guarantee that a message won't be delivered more than once during the visibility timeout period." A worker that is still waiting on a slow LLM response when the visibility timeout (default 30s) expires without deleting the message causes SQS to redeliver that same message — a second, genuine LLM call that MessageDeduplicationId cannot see, because no second SendMessage was ever issued to check an ID against. LLM calls routinely exceed 30 seconds, so this redelivery path is plausibly the larger source of duplicate calls in an SQS-fronted LLM pipeline, and it sits entirely outside what this feature covers. The brief's note ("stops a duplicate LLM call before it is ever sent") is true only for the narrow producer-retry class it actually quotes — it is not a general dedup guarantee for the architecture, and a team relying on it alone will still double-call the model via redelivery. Secondary trap: content-based dedup hashes only the message body, not attributes — two requests that differ solely in attributes (e.g., model/version routing metadata) will collapse into one enqueue, a correctness risk in the opposite direction.
recovered.savings: UNQUANTIFIED — bounded by the rate of ambiguous producer-side SendMessage retries landing inside the 5-minute window; each one avoided is exactly one full LLM call saved. Does not extend to consumer-side redelivery duplicates (visibility timeout expiring mid-LLM-call), which is structurally unaddressed and plausibly the larger duplicate-call source in practice.
recovered.provenance: primary-doc (AWS SQS Developer Guide, both the FIFO exactly-once-processing page and the visibility-timeout page) for the mechanism itself; the application of it to "avoiding a duplicate LLM call" is inferred — an architectural pattern a customer would wire up themselves, not documented by AWS or any LLM provider as a cost-saving technique.
recovered.telemetrySignal: Not observable by inspecting model traffic alone. SQS publishes no "duplicates suppressed" CloudWatch metric. A content-blind audit could only infer suppressed enqueue-duplicates indirectly, by diffing the producer's own SendMessage call/retry log against the queue's NumberOfMessagesSent metric — a gap implies dedup fired. It cannot, from outside, distinguish "dedup prevented a second LLM call" from "the retry just never happened."
recovered.verifiedAgainst: 2026-08-17 (read date; docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues-exactly-once-processing.html shows no page-level revision/last-updated date; cross-checked against the sqs-visibility-timeout.html page, same guide, same read date)
recovered.quoteNow: "If you retry the SendMessage action within the 5-minute deduplication interval, Amazon SQS doesn't introduce any duplicates into the queue."
recovered.trap: "Exactly-once processing" names the enqueue-side guarantee only. AWS's own visibility-timeout docs concede FIFO queues are still at-least-once on delivery ("no absolute guarantee that a message won't be delivered more than once during the visibility timeout period") — so a worker whose LLM call outlasts the visibility timeout gets redelivered and calls the model again, a duplicate MessageDeduplicationId never sees.
recovered.settlingExperiment: Run a worker with visibility timeout set below typical LLM p50 latency (e.g., 10s against a call that takes 20s+), with request-id logging on every actual LLM invocation. Confirm SQS's NumberOfMessagesSent stays flat under repeated identical SendMessage retries (proves the enqueue-dedup claim), while the LLM invocation log still shows a second call per message once the visibility timeout is undersized (proves the redelivery gap the dedup ID doesn't cover).
recovered.verdictChangeReason: Verdict held at PASS_ABSOLUTE — the quoted mechanism is real, structural, and independently testable (not merely vendor-asserted), so it clears CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, and the surviving request is unmodified, so it clears the FAIL bar. What changed from the brief is scope, not verdict: the note's framing ("stops a duplicate LLM call before it is ever sent") is corrected from a general claim to the narrow producer-retry case the quote actually supports, with the at-least-once/visibility-timeout gap now named as the condition under which the protection does not apply.

recovered.name: Reservation amortization (pure accounting)
recovered.verdictChangeReason: Brief's PASS_ABSOLUTE holds and is now backed by a stronger structural point than the brief cited: amortization isn't just "recognition-timing," it's a Cost Management reporting computation that runs entirely after the fact over stored billing records — no request to the model is generated or altered by it, so there's no "wire" for it to touch at all. Confirmed the mechanism also applies, unmodified, to Microsoft Foundry PTU reservations specifically (separate dedicated doc, same math), which sharpens the brief's note rather than contradicting it.
recovered.reasoning: Amortization is a Cost Management reporting lens applied after the fact to a reservation/savings-plan purchase already on the books: it re-slices a fixed one-time or monthly payment into daily/monthly amounts and reallocates it across the resources (or PTU deployments) that consumed it, purely for chargeback/showback. It never touches a request — the model reads the identical prompt, the identical model answers, and the identical amount of thinking happens, regardless of which cost metric (Actual vs Amortized) a billing admin later selects in the portal or API. Doc: "Amortization is the process of breaking the one-time cost into periodic costs" and, in a separate paragraph, "Amortized costs are available only for reservations and savings plans" (learn.microsoft.com/.../view-amortized-costs, ms.date 2026-07-17, read 2026-08-17). The same page confirms the bill itself is untouched: the Actual-cost view "shows the purchase as it appears on your bill... You will see the same monthly charge on your invoice as well" — amortized cost is a second lens on the same underlying charge, never a different charge. Applies identically to Microsoft Foundry Provisioned Throughput (PTU) reservations: the dedicated PTU page (.../reservations/microsoft-foundry, same ms.date) has its own "Monthly amortized costs" section doing the identical day-splitting arithmetic on a PTU reservation's fixed monthly cost ($200/31 in May, $200/28 in February) — same mechanism, same non-effect on what's billed or served. Trap: this earns PASS_ABSOLUTE only because zero bytes change on the wire; the moment someone sells "amortize your PTU reservation" as a way to *reduce* spend rather than *time-shift its recognition*, that's exactly the bait the brief flagged — no discount, no different tokens, just a different column in a spreadsheet. It stops holding only if Azure ever let the amortized-cost metric feed back into PTU reservation matching or hourly billing decisions; nothing in either page describes that, and the architecture (Cost Management/Billing API reading post-hoc usage exports) makes it structurally unlikely.
recovered.savings: None. Amortization reallocates the timing and resource-attribution of an already-fixed reservation/PTU-reservation payment; it does not reduce what is paid — the invoice total is identical under Actual and Amortized views. (The reservation purchase itself can cut PTU cost vs. hourly pay-as-you-go, per Microsoft's separate PTU reservation pricing material, but that's the discount from *committing*, not a product of amortization, which is a pure reporting/chargeback split of that already-fixed cost.)
recovered.telemetrySignal: Not observable at the inference wire, and that's structural, not a gap: amortization is computed after the fact from stored billing/usage-export records inside the Cost Management/Billing API (Actual cost vs Amortized cost metrics, UnusedReservation/UnusedSavingsPlan charge types) — nothing in a chat-completions or PTU-deployment request/response reflects it. A content-blind audit of model traffic would see identical requests, responses, latencies, and token counts whether or not amortization was ever viewed; the only place it's visible is a billing-export diff showing the same total reservation cost reallocated across days/resources, never a change to what was served.
recovered.quoteNow: "*Amortization* is the process of breaking the one-time cost into periodic costs." ... "Amortized costs are available only for reservations and savings plans. They aren't available for Azure Marketplace purchases." (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/reservations/view-amortized-costs, ms.date 2026-07-17). Corroborating, on invoice-identity: "Actual cost - Shows the purchase as it appears on your bill... You will see the same monthly charge on your invoice as well." PTU-specific corroboration (.../reservations/microsoft-foundry, ms.date 2026-07-17): "Your amortized reservation cost is based on each calendar month... If your cost for a monthly reservation is $200 and: The reservation was purchased in May, then you see daily the amortized cost of $200/31."
recovered.trap: Reads as "amortization saves you money" if the "breaking...into periodic costs" framing is heard as a discount rather than a recognition-timing/chargeback split; the invoice total is unchanged, so any pitch that quantifies "savings" from amortization itself (as opposed to from the reservation purchase decision) is selling a relabeled cost, not a smaller one.
recovered.settlingExperiment: Diff PTU deployment inference requests/responses and hourly reservation-matching/billing decisions with Cost Management's metric toggled between "Actual cost" and "Amortized cost" — expect byte-identical inference traffic and identical hourly reservation coverage in both cases, since amortization only reads stored usage/billing records after the fact and writes nothing back into the metering or serving path.

recovered.name: gRPC retry throttling (token-bucket retry budget)
recovered.verdictChangeReason: Brief read "paused" as a pure scheduling deferral (retry sent later, same eventual outcome). gRFC A6 — the spec grpc.io's page summarizes — says the opposite in plain language: throttled retry attempts are canceled and the failure is returned to the application immediately, not delayed. That's an outcome change (error now vs. a retry that might have succeeded), not a timing change, and it's exactly the case the bar's own definition of FAIL is written for: the savings exist only on the calls whose product changed.
recovered.reasoning: Mechanism, at the level the client actually executes it: the gRPC client keeps one token_count per server name, starting at maxTokens; every failed RPC costs 1 token, every success refunds tokenRatio. grpc.io: "If the token_count falls below half of maxTokens, retries are paused until the count recovers." Read alone, "paused" sounds like PASS_SCHEDULING — same retry, later. gRFC A6 (github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A6-client-retries.md, "Implemented," last updated 2024-08-23) removes the ambiguity: "If token_count is less than or equal to the threshold... RPCs will not be retried until token_count rises over the threshold" — and explicitly, throttled "retry attempts are canceled and failures returned to the application; hedged requests are also canceled." Nothing is rescheduled. The caller gets an error now instead of a retry that had some nonzero chance of succeeding. The token bucket has no way to tell a retry that was doomed anyway (pure waste, genuinely avoided) from one that would have gone through (service denied, not saved) — it only tracks aggregate recent failure rate. So whenever this mechanism actually does something — outside the trigger window it saves nothing, behaving exactly like plain retry — it is by construction suppressing some calls that would otherwise have completed. That is "a changed product sold as a saving," the bar's own FAIL condition, not a timing artifact. It stops holding as even a candidate for the register's scope at all: Anthropic and OpenAI expose HTTP/REST, not gRPC, so this budget lives inside a gRPC channel neither vendor ever sees or offers — it's only reachable if the customer builds and operates their own gRPC-to-HTTP gateway in front of the vendor's API, making the "provider" here the gRPC project, not a frontier LLM vendor. And even behind such a gateway it is one client process's own aggregate budget per server name — it throttles a single caller's retry storm, not the many-caller thundering herd that register #158 already named as the real, unsolved problem. Both caveats the brief raised survive into this entry; neither is a footnote, both are why the ceiling is low regardless of the verdict letter.
recovered.savings: None as a clean efficiency gain. Every dollar it "saves" is a suppressed retry that either would have failed anyway (real waste avoided, size unmeasured — depends on backend failure-rate distribution during the specific outage) or would have succeeded (service denied, not saved, and indistinguishable from the first case by the token bucket itself). Applies at all only behind a self-run gRPC gateway, which the typical hosted-API customer of Anthropic or OpenAI does not operate.
recovered.provenance: primary-doc — grpc.io official guide plus the gRFC A6 specification it summarizes (github.com/grpc/proposal), both fetched and cross-checked directly; neither is authored by a frontier LLM provider, since none exposes this surface.
recovered.telemetrySignal: Not observable from outside the customer's own process. A throttled retry never leaves the gRPC client, so there is no request on the wire and nothing a provider-side or network-level content-blind audit could see. The only trace is in the customer's own client-side OpenTelemetry metrics (grpc.client.attempt.started flattening while error counts keep climbing) — auditing it requires instrumentation access to the customer's own channel, not the provider-facing wire.
recovered.verifiedAgainst: grpc.io/docs/guides/retry/, page footer states "Last modified November 26, 2025"; read 2026-08-17. Cross-checked against github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A6-client-retries.md ("Last Updated: August 23, 2024"); read 2026-08-17.
recovered.quoteNow: "For each server, the gRPC client tracks a token_count (initially set to maxTokens). Failed RPCs decrement the count by 1, successful RPCs increment it by tokenRatio. If the token_count falls below half of maxTokens, retries are paused until the count recovers."
recovered.trap: "Paused" reads as delayed; the spec says canceled. The bucket can't tell a doomed retry from one that would have succeeded, so the "savings" quietly include denied service — and the only two providers in scope don't speak gRPC at all, so the mechanism has almost no floor to stand on before it even gets to that problem.
recovered.settlingExperiment: Point a self-hosted grpc-gateway at a backend forced to fail >50% of calls, trip the throttle, and watch grpc.client.attempt.started plateau while the application receives immediate errors with no further attempts recorded — confirms cancellation, not delay, directly from the client's own metrics rather than from the doc's wording.

recovered.name: Team/Enterprise per-seat pricing as the sanctioned alternative to account sharing
recovered.reasoning: A seat license is an authorization/quota wrapper in front of claude.ai — it decides who may open a session and how much monthly usage they're allotted, but it sits upstream of the inference call and is invisible to the model: the prompt tokens the model reads, which model answers, and how much it thinks are identical whether the human typing holds an individually-billed seat or (the ToS-violating alternative) a shared login. The page's own words close the loop — "Seat price + usage at API rates — $20/seat. Usage cost scales with model and task" — meaning usage above the seat fee is metered on the same schedule as a bare API key, not some seat-discounted rate, and nothing on the page describes Team/Enterprise routing to dedicated or priority capacity the way Azure/Bedrock PTU explicitly does. That's why this sits with the Anthropic committed-spend entry (register id 110, PASS_ABSOLUTE: "identical model, identical request, identical tokens — only the negotiated price differs") rather than the PTU/Reserved-Tier cap class (ids 89, 103, 107, 108, 112, 113 — all CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, because execution there genuinely moves to a separate dedicated/reserved fleet the provider asserts but the customer can't independently verify). It would stop holding the moment Anthropic documents Enterprise seats being routed to reserved or priority infrastructure — Max already sells "priority access" as an individual add-on, so the precedent for that move exists. The trap: "$20/seat" reads like a price ceiling; it's a licensing floor with full, undiscounted API-rate usage stacked on top, and Premium's 5x-cost seat buys usage headroom, not a different or better answer — so the entry carries zero token-savings content. It's the price of not sharing a password.
recovered.savings: None as a token-cost lever. Per-seat pricing is strictly more expensive than the ToS-violating shared-login alternative it replaces: Team Standard $20/seat/mo (annual, $25 monthly), Team Premium $100/seat/mo (annual, $125 monthly, "5x more usage than standard seats"), for 2-150 seats; Enterprise $20/seat plus usage explicitly billed "at API rates" with no stated seat-linked discount. Premium's 5x figure is a usage-quota expansion, not a per-token price break. The only real number here is compliance cost, not savings.
recovered.telemetrySignal: Detectable only from account/billing metadata — seat count, seat tier (Standard/Premium/Enterprise), and org SSO/SCIM configuration are contract-level facts visible to a content-blind auditor. There is no per-request signal: seat tier never appears in the request path (no header, no routing difference) because it is pure access provisioning sitting in front of, not inside, the inference call.
recovered.quoteNow: Team — Standard seat: "All Claude features, plus more usage than Pro* $20 Per seat / month if billed annually. $25 if billed monthly." Premium seat: "5x more usage than standard seats* $100 Per seat / month if billed annually. $125 if billed monthly." Team size: "For teams of 2 to 150." Enterprise: "Seat price + usage at API rates — $20/seat. Usage cost scales with model and task." Footnote: "Prices shown don't include applicable tax. Price and plans are subject to change at Anthropic's discretion." (No sentence anywhere on the page addresses one-account-per-person or credential/seat sharing.)
recovered.trap: "$20/seat" reads like the whole bill; it's the access fee, and every token above it bills at plain API rates with no seat-linked discount — the "saving" here is ToS compliance, not tokens.
recovered.verdictChangeReason: The brief filed this in "the same cap class the register already applies to batch and PTU" and called it CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. But checking the actual register (docs/research/2026-08-10-verdicts-final.json) shows that cap class is not uniform: the PTU/Reserved-Tier entries (ids 89, 103, 107, 108, 112, 113) get CONTRACTUAL_ONLY specifically because execution moves to a separate dedicated/reserved fleet whose byte-identical equivalence rests on the provider's word. Anthropic's own committed-spend entry (id 110) gets PASS_ABSOLUTE instead, reasoned as "a pure commercial/contractual lever: identical model, identical request, identical tokens — only the negotiated price differs." Team/Enterprise per-seat licensing matches id 110's shape, not the PTU family's: nothing on claude.com/pricing describes dedicated or separate serving infrastructure for Team/Enterprise, and Enterprise usage is explicitly billed "at API rates" — the same meter as a standalone key. There is no provider assertion here to take on faith, so CONTRACTUAL_ONLY was the wrong bucket; changed to PASS_ABSOLUTE.
recovered.settlingExperiment: Not needed — settled structurally by the absence of any dedicated/reserved-capacity language on the pricing page plus the explicit "usage at API rates" clause for Enterprise. Would need re-checking only if Anthropic later documents Team/Enterprise seats routed to separate infrastructure (e.g., a future "priority processing" claim for Enterprise mirroring what Max already sells individually as "priority access").

recovered.name: Azure PTU Reservations — exit and cancellation mechanics
recovered.reasoning:
Mechanism: exit/cancellation terms don't touch what the model reads at all — canceling, exchanging, or holding a PTU reservation changes nothing about the request, the deployment, or the model; it only changes who pays what. So the whole question is a billing-contract fact, not a serving fact. Microsoft's PTU billing doc labels the reservation "Cancelable, with limits | Reservations can be canceled or exchanged after purchase, but those actions might incur fees" (provisioned-throughput-billing, ms.date 2026-05-22 — unchanged since the brief). The general Azure Reservations exchange/refund page supplies the limits (ms.date 2026-07-22, also unchanged): "The total canceled commitment can't exceed 50,000 USD in a 12-month rolling window for a billing profile or single enrollment," and on fees: "We're currently not charging an early termination fee, but in the future there might be a 12% early termination fee for cancellations." (The brief's ETF fragment was a light paraphrase dressed in quotes — this is the verbatim sentence; substance is unchanged.)

Every one of these is a documentation sentence about Microsoft's own billing system — no request was ever sent, nothing measurable, only Microsoft's word that the $50k pool and 12% figure are what actually gets enforced. recovered.name: PromptXRay (karminski) — read-only cache-hit diagnostic
recovered.verdictChangeReason: Brief stopped at INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE because it treated the README's "never rewrites" line as unverifiable self-description. Reading the actual source (gateway.py, litellm_callback.py) upgrades this to a structural argument, which the register's own rules accept in place of a live-traffic test: gateway.py's proxy path builds the upstream call as client.stream(method, url, headers=forwarded_headers, content=raw_body) — raw_body is the exact byte string captured from the customer's own client, never re-parsed or re-serialized; the LiteLLM integration path (async_pre_call_hook) is the same shape and returns data unchanged. Nothing that becomes model input is touched in either path. But _forward_headers() DOES rewrite real bytes on the wire — it strips hop-by-hop headers and Host, and relocates Authorization into x-api-key for BYOK credential routing, adding an x-promptxray-request-id tag — none of which a model ever tokenizes (vendor feature-flag headers like anthropic-version/anthropic-beta pass through unmodified since the filter is a stoplist, not an allowlist). That combination — body bit-identical, only never-read fields altered — is the definition of PASS_METADATA, not the stronger PASS_ABSOLUTE (the wire is not literally unchanged) and stronger than the brief's INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE (the claim is no longer resting on the author's word alone).
recovered.reasoning:
Mechanism, at the level of what the model reads: gateway.py forwards the upstream request as client.stream(scope.get("method","POST"), url, headers=forwarded_headers, content=raw_body) — raw_body is the untouched byte string PromptXRay received, so the token sequence a downstream model tokenizes is bit-identical to what the customer's own client sent. _forward_headers() is a stoplist (hop-by-hop: connection/keep-alive/proxy-authenticate/proxy-authorization/te/trailers/transfer-encoding/upgrade; plus host; plus the auth trio authorization/x-api-key/api-key, relocated for BYOK routing), not an allowlist, so every other header — including provider feature-flag headers that could change how much a model thinks — passes through unmodified. The LiteLLM integration path is the same shape: async_pre_call_hook(...) -> dict returns data unchanged. Response-side work (analysis.py's analyze_pair prefix-diffing, window_analysis.py's provider_cache_gap check) runs only after client.stream() returns, dispatched via self.writer.submit() — strictly post-hoc, outside the hot path. So: same tokens, same model, same amount of thinking; only transport plumbing the model never sees is altered.

refutations.name: K8s CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Forbid/Replace
refutations.reason:
Quote checks out verbatim (fetched kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/ live on 2026-08-17): Forbid text matches exactly, and the idempotency-caveat quote ("A CronJob creates a Job object approximately once... the Jobs that you define should be idempotent") is also verbatim. But the verdict doesn't survive the checklist.

Item 2 is the kill shot: "Is there any path where it suppresses a call that would NOT have been a true duplicate?" — Yes, and the reasoning admits it in the same breath it grants PASS_ABSOLUTE: "The check is Job-status/time-only, never content-aware, so it cannot distinguish 'redundant duplicate' from 'distinct work that happens to overlap.'" Forbid is a scheduling-level "is a Job object active" check, not a request-dedup check. It has no visibility into whether the overlapping run would have processed the same queue item, the same batch, the same prompt — or a completely different one. K8s' own docs put the burden on the user ("the Jobs that you define should be idempotent") rather than guaranteeing it, which is Kubernetes declining to promise the exact property the PASS_ABSOLUTE verdict needs. A mechanism whose safety depends on an assumption about the caller's workload — one the platform explicitly disclaims enforcing — is not a structural "nothing on the wire changed" guarantee; it's conditionally true only for a subclass of deployments (provably idempotent jobs), which the entry as written doesn't scope to. For any CronJob whose "duplicate" run would in fact have done distinct work, Forbid silently drops that work — a different amount of thinking happens (zero, instead of some) for that invocation, which is the FAIL condition in the register's own bar, not a neutral no-op.

The Replace half is worse, and self-refuting within the reasoning itself: it concedes that "a kill-after-dispatch pays for the discarded run's tokens on top of the replacement's, which is a cost increase, not a saving, in that window." For any LLM call with nontrivial latency (which is most of them), the window where the old Pod has already dispatched its HTTP request before the new Pod's kill signal lands is not an edge case — it's the common case for long-running jobs, which is exactly when overlap-driven replacement is likely to fire. In that path, MORE tokens go out, not zero — directly contradicting "nothing on the wire changed." Bundling Replace under the same PASS_ABSOLUTE verdict as Forbid, when the reasoning's own text shows Replace routinely fails the bar, means the entry as stated overclaims.

Net: this isn't a case where a documentation sentence is being mistaken for proof (the structural argument — no Job object, no Pod, no process, no HTTP call — is legitimate and does support PASS_ABSOLUTE in principle, unlike provider-promise entries that cap at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY). The flaw is scope: the entry claims a blanket PASS_ABSOLUTE for "Forbid/Replace" as a category, but (a) Forbid's "no duplicate spend" property is content-blind and only true under an idempotency assumption Kubernetes explicitly declines to guarantee, and (b) Replace demonstrably fails the "nothing changed" bar in the common kill-after-dispatch window, by the reasoning's own admission.
refutations.proposedVerdict: Split, not a blanket PASS_ABSOLUTE. Forbid: downgrade to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (or a PASS_ABSOLUTE scoped explicitly to "only when the workload is provably idempotent/duplicate-detecting" — a property of the user's job, not of the K8s primitive, which the docs decline to guarantee: "the Jobs that you define should be idempotent"). Replace: FAIL as a blanket claim — the reasoning's own kill-after-dispatch scenario shows extra tokens sent in the common case, so "nothing on the wire changed" does not hold generally.

refutations.name: BullMQ job deduplication (Simple Mode)
refutations.reason:
Sourcing checks out — I re-verified independently and the claim's citations are solid: the quote is verbatim on the live page (confirmed by direct curl, not just WebFetch's summary — the sentence "as long as the job remains in an incomplete state... any subsequent job with the same deduplication ID will be ignored" is there word for word), the Lua line numbers are exact (addStandardJob-9.lua:102-104 is literally `if deduplicationJobId then / return deduplicationJobId / end`, with storeJob at line 107 and addJobInTargetList at 114, strictly after), and GitHub metadata matches (pushed_at 2026-08-17T14:34:27Z, 9303 stars, MIT — all confirmed via the REST API). I also pulled deduplicateJobWithoutReplace.lua and storeDeduplicatedNextJob.lua to confirm the "discards it outright" characterization: in base Simple Mode (no ttl, no keepLastIfActive), storeDeduplicatedNextJob returns false unconditionally, so the second job's data is never persisted anywhere. The mechanism description is accurate, not a documentation claim dressed up as source.

But the verdict doesn't follow from the mechanism. Fetch the collision check itself: `deduplicationKeyExists = not rcall('SET', deduplicationKey, jobId, 'NX')`. That's a SET NX on a caller-supplied string key against a caller-supplied string value (jobId) — zero bytes of the job's actual payload enter the comparison. This directly answers your first check question: the mechanism is content-blind, confirmed in source, not inferred. It cannot distinguish "the same logical request retried" from "two different requests that happen to share a dedup ID" — it only ever checks whether a string was seen before.

That makes your second check question decisive: yes, there is a path where it suppresses a call that would NOT have been a true duplicate — and it's not a remote edge case, it's the entire mechanism, by design. BullMQ's own docs example uses an arbitrary app-level id (`{ id: 'customValue' }`) and pitches Simple Mode for "a critical update that should not be repeated if the initial attempt is still in progress" — note: not "an identical update," a critical update. The natural, encouraged usage is per-logical-task ID, not a hash of the payload. Nothing in the library enforces or checks that the ID is 1:1 with content. If a caller reuses a dedup ID across two distinct prompts while the first is still in flight, the second is silently discarded and the caller's `.add()` call resolves to the FIRST job's result — a different answer to a different question, returned as if it were fine.

The submitted reasoning actually concedes this in its own closing paragraph ("Get that wrong and the 'savings' isn't a skipped duplicate call, it's a silently dropped distinct request... a correctness bug wearing a savings entry's clothes") and then still asserts PASS_ABSOLUTE, treating the concession as a footnote about ROI-sizing rather than what it is: an admission that "nothing on the wire changed" is not a property of the library, it's a property of caller discipline the library neither verifies nor can verify. That's a categorically different, weaker guarantee than a genuine no-op case (e.g., a client cache keyed by a hash of the exact request bytes, where the "duplicate" determination is intrinsically content-derived and self-verifying). PASS_ABSOLUTE per the rubric requires the structural argument to hold unconditionally ("no request was ever sent" as a fact about the mechanism); here it only holds conditionally on an external invariant the mechanism does nothing to enforce, and the failure mode when that invariant breaks is exactly "a changed product sold as a saving" — the caller's actual distinct request never reaches the model at all, and they get someone else's answer back without being told. That's worse than ordinary FAIL (different tokens/different model), not milder than it, so I would not round it up to a conditional PASS — I'd fail it, or at most treat it as CONTRACTUAL_ONLY if the entry is rewritten to scope the claim to "content-derived dedup IDs only," which is not how the library ships or how its own example documents it.
refutations.proposedVerdict: FAIL (at best CONTRACTUAL_ONLY if reframed as "safe when the caller's dedup-ID scheme is content-derived" — but as shipped and as documented, not PASS_ABSOLUTE)

refutations.name: AWS SQS FIFO MessageDeduplicationId
refutations.reason:
Both quotes check out verbatim against the live pages as of 2026-08-17 (no revision date on either page), so this isn't a quote-drift finding. But the verdict itself doesn't survive the register's own evidentiary bar.

Primary refutation — documentation sentence treated as proof: The entire causal chain rests on one AWS prose sentence: "If you retry the SendMessage action within the 5-minute deduplication interval, Amazon SQS doesn't introduce any duplicates into the queue." That's a description of SQS's internal enqueue-time behavior — a black box the customer cannot inspect. There is no measurement in the entry (no count of SendMessage retries sent vs. messages actually delivered to a consumer, no CloudWatch metric check, nothing) and no architectural proof from outside AWS's control (e.g., client-side code that literally never issues the second network call — that's not what's happening here; the client DOES send the second SendMessage, and we're trusting AWS's word that it discards it server-side). The register's own rule is explicit and applies directly: "A documentation sentence is THE PROVIDER'S WORD, however clearly it reads, and caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY... Only a measurement or a structural argument... supports PASS_ABSOLUTE." This entry has neither — it has a doc quote dressed as a structural argument. That alone downgrades it to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (AWS asserts the dedup behavior; we cannot independently verify it without running the experiment ourselves, which wasn't done here).

Secondary finding — the mechanism can suppress a genuine (non-duplicate) call, contrary to "does it suppress a call that would NOT have been a true duplicate?": The entry's own "secondary trap" only flags content-based dedup's blindness to attributes. But the claim's title is "MessageDeduplicationId" — the explicit-ID mode, not content-based dedup. In explicit mode, SQS compares only the developer-supplied ID string; it does not hash or compare the body at all. Two calls with genuinely different bodies (a real second, distinct request, not a retry) that happen to share an explicit dedup ID by producer bug or ID-reuse get silently collapsed into one enqueued message — the second, legitimately different LLM call never gets sent, and no error surfaces. That's a stronger version of the same failure mode the entry already partially conceded, and it means "exactly one, byte-identical LLM request goes out" is not even true for all traffic through this feature, only for the narrow honest-retry-with-identical-body case the entry cherry-picked.

Both points support the same direction: demote from PASS_ABSOLUTE to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. The visibility-timeout redelivery caveat the entry already includes is a correct and separate point but doesn't need re-litigating — the documentation-sentence cap alone is sufficient to refute PASS_ABSOLUTE.

refutations.name: PromptXRay (karminski) — read-only cache-hit diagnostic
refutations.reason:
Mechanism, at the level of what the model actually reads: the reviewed reasoning stops at gateway.py's `client.stream(..., content=raw_body)` and calls that "bit-identical to what the customer's own client sent" — but that call's target is `url = f"{self.config.internal_base_url}{endpoint}"`, and `internal_base_url` is `http://127.0.0.1:7411`, a local LiteLLM subprocess that `runtime.py`'s `serve()` always spawns (`LiteLLMProcess(config).start()` before `uvicorn.run(GatewayApp(...))`). There is no code path where gateway.py calls the real upstream directly. `generate_litellm_config()` hardcodes every model through LiteLLM's own "openai" provider adapter regardless of what the real backend is: `{"model_name": "*", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/*", "api_base": config.upstream_base_url, ...}}`. So raw_body reaching the internal port proves nothing about what reaches the model — the actual outbound body is rebuilt by litellm's `OpenAIGPTConfig.transform_request()` (pinned `litellm[proxy]==1.91.2` in pyproject.toml), and that function is not a pass-through.

Quote that decided it (litellm v1.91.2, `litellm/llms/openai/chat/gpt_transformation.py`, read 2026-08-17): `transform_request()` calls `self._transform_messages(...)`, which unconditionally rewrites `image_url` string content into dict form, and `_handle_pdf_url()` — `base64_data = convert_url_to_base64(file_id); content_copy["file_data"] = base64_data; content_copy.pop("file_id")` — actively fetches a referenced PDF URL client-side and replaces the reference with fetched, re-encoded bytes before the request ever leaves the machine. The same function also runs `remove_cache_control_flag_from_messages_and_tools()`, stripping `cache_control` breakpoint hints from messages/tools whenever the resolved hostname is `openai.com`/`*.openai.com`. And `get_supported_openai_params(model)` gates params like `user` on whether `model` is literally inside litellm's own hardcoded `litellm.open_ai_chat_completion_models` list — which self-hosted / non-canonical "OpenAI-compatible" model names (exactly PromptXRay's stated market: the README pitches it at "OpenAI 兼容API," the ecosystem of self-hosted/third-party endpoints, not openai.com itself) will not be in, so params present in the client's original request are silently absent from what reaches the provider.

None of this is hypothetical or version-agnostic guesswork: it is the pinned dependency's actual `transform_request()`, the single function that serializes the JSON body sent upstream, for every request PromptXRay proxies (since `model: "openai/*"` routes unconditionally through it). The README's "只读：绝不为优化缓存而改写请求或响应" is accurate as a statement of PromptXRay's own two files' intent, but it describes design intent for code the authors wrote, not a technical property of the mandatory LiteLLM hop sitting between gateway.py and the provider — a hop the original reasoning never opened.

Condition under which the strict "bit-identical" framing survives: pure single/multi-turn text chat completions, no image or file content blocks, targeting a model name litellm recognizes as canonical-OpenAI (or one that only uses params in `OpenAIGPTConfig.get_supported_openai_params`'s base list), against a non-openai.com host so `cache_control` is preserved. For that narrow slice, message content and param values likely survive semantically (though re-serialized, not byte-identical). Outside it — any PDF `file_id` reference, any string-form `image_url`, any client-set `cache_control` hint sent to an actual openai.com-hostnamed target, or any param whose litellm support is gated on a model name that isn't in litellm's hardcoded canonical list — the bytes and in the PDF case the actual referenced content the model reads provably differ from what the client sent. Neither the reviewed reasoning nor this check performed a live-traffic capture proving the narrow slice is what real PromptXRay users hit in practice; that gap is exactly what's needed to safely land back on PASS_METADATA for a qualified claim.

Trap: verifying only the two files with PromptXRay's own name on them (gateway.py, litellm_callback.py) and treating "reaches an internal URL unmodified" as "reaches the model unmodified," when the actual request-to-the-provider is built by a separate, unaudited third-party dependency that this repo's own runtime.py makes mandatory and unconditional for every proxied call. Same failure shape as sweep 12's paraphrase-as-quote: trusting the part of the pipeline that was convenient to read (raw_body forward, `return data` in the LiteLLM callback hook, which only proves PromptXRay's own logging hook doesn't mutate `data` further) while skipping the part that's actually load-bearing for "what tokens does the model read" (LiteLLM's own `transform_request`).

SOURCE: promptxray repo — 2026-07-11 (75ccf503, only commit, confirmed unchanged via `gh api repos/karminski/PromptXRay/commits`), read 2026-08-17 (README.md, src/promptxray/gateway.py, litellm_callback.py, config.py, runtime.py, advisor.py, pyproject.toml, tests/test_gateway.py, tests/test_litellm_integration.py, api.github.com/repos/karminski/PromptXRay). litellm dependency — tag v1.91.2 exists and matches the exact pin in promptxray's pyproject.toml; read 2026-08-17 (raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/v1.91.2/litellm/llms/openai/chat/gpt_transformation.py).
refutations.proposedVerdict: FAIL (downgrade from PASS_METADATA; if the register wants a narrower claim scoped to plain-text-only traffic on canonical model names, INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is the fallback — but the claim as written is unqualified and is falsified)

Item 2 is the kill shot: "Is there any path where it suppresses a call that would NOT have been a true duplicate?" — Yes, and the reasoning admits it in the same breath it grants PASS_ABSOLUTE: "The check is Job-status/time-only, never content-aware, so it cannot distinguish 'redundant duplicate' from 'distinct work that happens to overlap.'" Forbid is a scheduling-level "is a Job object active" check, not a request-dedup check. It has no visibility into whether the overlapping run would have processed the same queue item, the same batch, the same prompt — or a completely different one. K8s' own docs put the burden on the user ("the Jobs that you define should be idempotent") rather than guaranteeing it, which is Kubernetes declining to promise the exact property the PASS_ABSOLUTE verdict needs. A mechanism whose safety depends on an assumption about the caller's workload — one the platform explicitly disclaims enforcing — is not a structural "nothing on the wire changed" guarantee; it's conditionally true only for a subclass of deployments (provably idempotent jobs), which the entry as written doesn't scope to. For any CronJob whose "duplicate" run would in fact have done distinct work, Forbid silently drops that work — a different amount of thinking happens (zero, instead of some) for that invocation, which is the FAIL condition in the register's own bar, not a neutral no-op.

The Replace half is worse, and self-refuting within the reasoning itself: it concedes that "a kill-after-dispatch pays for the discarded run's tokens on top of the replacement's, which is a cost increase, not a saving, in that window." For any LLM call with nontrivial latency (which is most of them), the window where the old Pod has already dispatched its HTTP request before the new Pod's kill signal lands is not an edge case — it's the common case for long-running jobs, which is exactly when overlap-driven replacement is likely to fire. In that path, MORE tokens go out, not zero — directly contradicting "nothing on the wire changed." Bundling Replace under the same PASS_ABSOLUTE verdict as Forbid, when the reasoning's own text shows Replace routinely fails the bar, means the entry as stated overclaims.

Net: this isn't a case where a documentation sentence is being mistaken for proof (the structural argument — no Job object, no Pod, no process, no HTTP call — is legitimate and does support PASS_ABSOLUTE in principle, unlike provider-promise entries that cap at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY). The flaw is scope: the entry claims a blanket PASS_ABSOLUTE for "Forbid/Replace" as a category, but (a) Forbid's "no duplicate spend" property is content-blind and only true under an idempotency assumption Kubernetes explicitly declines to guarantee, and (b) Replace demonstrably fails the "nothing changed" bar in the common kill-after-dispatch window, by the reasoning's own admission.
killed.proposedVerdict: Split, not a blanket PASS_ABSOLUTE. Forbid: downgrade to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (or a PASS_ABSOLUTE scoped explicitly to "only when the workload is provably idempotent/duplicate-detecting" — a property of the user's job, not of the K8s primitive, which the docs decline to guarantee: "the Jobs that you define should be idempotent"). Replace: FAIL as a blanket claim — the reasoning's own kill-after-dispatch scenario shows extra tokens sent in the common case, so "nothing on the wire changed" does not hold generally.

I also pulled deduplicateJobWithoutReplace.lua and storeDeduplicatedNextJob.lua to confirm the "discards it outright" characterization: in base Simple Mode (no ttl, no keepLastIfActive), storeDeduplicatedNextJob returns false unconditionally, so the second job's data is never persisted anywhere. The mechanism description is accurate, not a documentation claim dressed up as source.

But the verdict doesn't follow from the mechanism. Fetch the collision check itself: `deduplicationKeyExists = not rcall('SET', deduplicationKey, jobId, 'NX')`. That's a SET NX on a caller-supplied string key against a caller-supplied string value (jobId) — zero bytes of the job's actual payload enter the comparison. This directly answers your first check question: the mechanism is content-blind, confirmed in source, not inferred. It cannot distinguish "the same logical request retried" from "two different requests that happen to share a dedup ID" — it only ever checks whether a string was seen before.

That makes your second check question decisive: yes, there is a path where it suppresses a call that would NOT have been a true duplicate — and it's not a remote edge case, it's the entire mechanism, by design. BullMQ's own docs example uses an arbitrary app-level id (`{ id: 'customValue' }`) and pitches Simple Mode for "a critical update that should not be repeated if the initial attempt is still in progress" — note: not "an identical update," a critical update. The natural, encouraged usage is per-logical-task ID, not a hash of the payload. Nothing in the library enforces or checks that the ID is 1:1 with content. If a caller reuses a dedup ID across two distinct prompts while the first is still in flight, the second is silently discarded and the caller's `.add()` call resolves to the FIRST job's result — a different answer to a different question, returned as if it were fine.

The submitted reasoning actually concedes this in its own closing paragraph ("Get that wrong and the 'savings' isn't a skipped duplicate call, it's a silently dropped distinct request... a correctness bug wearing a savings entry's clothes") and then still asserts PASS_ABSOLUTE, treating the concession as a footnote about ROI-sizing rather than what it is: an admission that "nothing on the wire changed" is not a property of the library, it's a property of caller discipline the library neither verifies nor can verify. That's a categorically different, weaker guarantee than a genuine no-op case (e.g., a client cache keyed by a hash of the exact request bytes, where the "duplicate" determination is intrinsically content-derived and self-verifying). PASS_ABSOLUTE per the rubric requires the structural argument to hold unconditionally ("no request was ever sent" as a fact about the mechanism); here it only holds conditionally on an external invariant the mechanism does nothing to enforce, and the failure mode when that invariant breaks is exactly "a changed product sold as a saving" — the caller's actual distinct request never reaches the model at all, and they get someone else's answer back without being told. That's worse than ordinary FAIL (different tokens/different model), not milder than it, so I would not round it up to a conditional PASS — I'd fail it, or at most treat it as CONTRACTUAL_ONLY if the entry is rewritten to scope the claim to "content-derived dedup IDs only," which is not how the library ships or how its own example documents it.
killed.proposedVerdict: FAIL (at best CONTRACTUAL_ONLY if reframed as "safe when the caller's dedup-ID scheme is content-derived" — but as shipped and as documented, not PASS_ABSOLUTE)

killed.name: AWS SQS FIFO MessageDeduplicationId
killed.reason:
Both quotes check out verbatim against the live pages as of 2026-08-17 (no revision date on either page), so this isn't a quote-drift finding. But the verdict itself doesn't survive the register's own evidentiary bar.

Primary refutation — documentation sentence treated as proof: The entire causal chain rests on one AWS prose sentence: "If you retry the SendMessage action within the 5-minute deduplication interval, Amazon SQS doesn't introduce any duplicates into the queue." That's a description of SQS's internal enqueue-time behavior — a black box the customer cannot inspect. There is no measurement in the entry (no count of SendMessage retries sent vs. messages actually delivered to a consumer, no CloudWatch metric check, nothing) and no architectural proof from outside AWS's control (e.g., client-side code that literally never issues the second network call — that's not what's happening here; the client DOES send the second SendMessage, and we're trusting AWS's word that it discards it server-side). The register's own rule is explicit and applies directly: "A documentation sentence is THE PROVIDER'S WORD, however clearly it reads, and caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY... Only a measurement or a structural argument... supports PASS_ABSOLUTE." This entry has neither — it has a doc quote dressed as a structural argument. That alone downgrades it to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (AWS asserts the dedup behavior; we cannot independently verify it without running the experiment ourselves, which wasn't done here).

Secondary finding — the mechanism can suppress a genuine (non-duplicate) call, contrary to "does it suppress a call that would NOT have been a true duplicate?": The entry's own "secondary trap" only flags content-based dedup's blindness to attributes. But the claim's title is "MessageDeduplicationId" — the explicit-ID mode, not content-based dedup. In explicit mode, SQS compares only the developer-supplied ID string; it does not hash or compare the body at all. Two calls with genuinely different bodies (a real second, distinct request, not a retry) that happen to share an explicit dedup ID by producer bug or ID-reuse get silently collapsed into one enqueued message — the second, legitimately different LLM call never gets sent, and no error surfaces. That's a stronger version of the same failure mode the entry already partially conceded, and it means "exactly one, byte-identical LLM request goes out" is not even true for all traffic through this feature, only for the narrow honest-retry-with-identical-body case the entry cherry-picked.

Both points support the same direction: demote from PASS_ABSOLUTE to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. The visibility-timeout redelivery caveat the entry already includes is a correct and separate point but doesn't need re-litigating — the documentation-sentence cap alone is sufficient to refute PASS_ABSOLUTE.

killed.name: PromptXRay (karminski) — read-only cache-hit diagnostic
killed.reason:
Mechanism, at the level of what the model actually reads: the reviewed reasoning stops at gateway.py's `client.stream(..., content=raw_body)` and calls that "bit-identical to what the customer's own client sent" — but that call's target is `url = f"{self.config.internal_base_url}{endpoint}"`, and `internal_base_url` is `http://127.0.0.1:7411`, a local LiteLLM subprocess that `runtime.py`'s `serve()` always spawns (`LiteLLMProcess(config).start()` before `uvicorn.run(GatewayApp(...))`). There is no code path where gateway.py calls the real upstream directly. `generate_litellm_config()` hardcodes every model through LiteLLM's own "openai" provider adapter regardless of what the real backend is: `{"model_name": "*", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/*", "api_base": config.upstream_base_url, ...}}`. So raw_body reaching the internal port proves nothing about what reaches the model — the actual outbound body is rebuilt by litellm's `OpenAIGPTConfig.transform_request()` (pinned `litellm[proxy]==1.91.2` in pyproject.toml), and that function is not a pass-through.

Quote that decided it (litellm v1.91.2, `litellm/llms/openai/chat/gpt_transformation.py`, read 2026-08-17): `transform_request()` calls `self._transform_messages(...)`, which unconditionally rewrites `image_url` string content into dict form, and `_handle_pdf_url()` — `base64_data = convert_url_to_base64(file_id); content_copy["file_data"] = base64_data; content_copy.pop("file_id")` — actively fetches a referenced PDF URL client-side and replaces the reference with fetched, re-encoded bytes before the request ever leaves the machine. The same function also runs `remove_cache_control_flag_from_messages_and_tools()`, stripping `cache_control` breakpoint hints from messages/tools whenever the resolved hostname is `openai.com`/`*.openai.com`. And `get_supported_openai_params(model)` gates params like `user` on whether `model` is literally inside litellm's own hardcoded `litellm.open_ai_chat_completion_models` list — which self-hosted / non-canonical "OpenAI-compatible" model names (exactly PromptXRay's stated market: the README pitches it at "OpenAI 兼容API," the ecosystem of self-hosted/third-party endpoints, not openai.com itself) will not be in, so params present in the client's original request are silently absent from what reaches the provider.

None of this is hypothetical or version-agnostic guesswork: it is the pinned dependency's actual `transform_request()`, the single function that serializes the JSON body sent upstream, for every request PromptXRay proxies (since `model: "openai/*"` routes unconditionally through it). The README's "只读：绝不为优化缓存而改写请求或响应" is accurate as a statement of PromptXRay's own two files' intent, but it describes design intent for code the authors wrote, not a technical property of the mandatory LiteLLM hop sitting between gateway.py and the provider — a hop the original reasoning never opened.

Condition under which the strict "bit-identical" framing survives: pure single/multi-turn text chat completions, no image or file content blocks, targeting a model name litellm recognizes as canonical-OpenAI (or one that only uses params in `OpenAIGPTConfig.get_supported_openai_params`'s base list), against a non-openai.com host so `cache_control` is preserved. For that narrow slice, message content and param values likely survive semantically (though re-serialized, not byte-identical). Outside it — any PDF `file_id` reference, any string-form `image_url`, any client-set `cache_control` hint sent to an actual openai.com-hostnamed target, or any param whose litellm support is gated on a model name that isn't in litellm's hardcoded canonical list — the bytes and in the PDF case the actual referenced content the model reads provably differ from what the client sent. Neither the reviewed reasoning nor this check performed a live-traffic capture proving the narrow slice is what real PromptXRay users hit in practice; that gap is exactly what's needed to safely land back on PASS_METADATA for a qualified claim.

Trap: verifying only the two files with PromptXRay's own name on them (gateway.py, litellm_callback.py) and treating "reaches an internal URL unmodified" as "reaches the model unmodified," when the actual request-to-the-provider is built by a separate, unaudited third-party dependency that this repo's own runtime.py makes mandatory and unconditional for every proxied call. Same failure shape as sweep 12's paraphrase-as-quote: trusting the part of the pipeline that was convenient to read (raw_body forward, `return data` in the LiteLLM callback hook, which only proves PromptXRay's own logging hook doesn't mutate `data` further) while skipping the part that's actually load-bearing for "what tokens does the model read" (LiteLLM's own `transform_request`).

**1. Single source, nobody cross-checked:**
Team/Enterprise pricing rests on claude.com/pricing alone — and that single source wasn't even fully read: markdown conversion dropped the "Priority access at high traffic times" table row, which is exactly what the refuter caught. No-EC2-RI-secondary-market cites only ri-market-general.html, no second page. **4. Not checked:**
The refutation pass only red-teamed the six entries claiming a pass — nobody checked whether any FAIL/CONTRACTUAL_ONLY/INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE verdict was too harsh, so the bias-check runs one direction only. Nobody ran an actual measurement for any PASS_ABSOLUTE claim (BullMQ, K8s Forbid/Replace) — every check was source-reading, never observed traffic through the mechanism. Nobody reconciled the three-way Azure citation overlap in point 3.
